items.followUp: Define fundamental quantities and give two examples.

rubric.why: This identifies what distinguishes a base quantity.
rubric.description: States that base quantities are independent of other quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for expressing that base quantities are not derived from other physical quantities.

rubric.why: This explains how derived quantities are formed.
rubric.description: States that derived quantities are obtained from base quantities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that derived quantities are formed by combining base quantities.

modelAnswer: Base quantities are independent physical quantities that are not derived from other quantities.
Derived quantities are obtained by combining base quantities.

items.followUp: State two rules for deciding whether a zero in a measurement is significant.

rubric.why: This is a standard rule for identifying significant digits.
rubric.description: States that all non-zero digits are significant.

rubric.why: This gives a second valid rule for identifying significant digits.
rubric.description: States that zeros between non-zero digits are significant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this rule; also accept another correct rule about zeros, such as leading zeros not being significant or trailing zeros after a decimal point being significant.

modelAnswer: All non-zero digits in a measurement are significant.
Zeros between non-zero digits are significant.

rubric.why: This states the defining form of scientific notation.
rubric.description: Defines scientific notation as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

rubric.why: A valid example demonstrates the notation.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of scientific notation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as 300,000,000 = 3.0 × 10⁸.

modelAnswer: Scientific notation expresses a number as a number between 1 and 10 multiplied by a power of 10.

items.followUp: Define static friction and kinetic friction.

rubric.why: This identifies friction as a force opposing motion or its tendency.
rubric.description: Defines friction as a force that opposes relative motion, or its tendency, between surfaces in contact.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition of friction.

rubric.why: Limiting friction is the maximum friction just before motion begins.
rubric.description: Defines limiting friction as the maximum frictional force just before a body starts moving.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition of limiting friction.

modelAnswer: Friction is the force that opposes the relative motion, or tendency of motion, between surfaces in contact.
Limiting friction is the maximum value of friction just before a body starts moving.

items.followUp: Where is the centre of gravity of a uniform circular disc?

rubric.why: This describes the centre of gravity in terms of the body's weight.
rubric.description: Identifies it as the point at which the body's weight acts or is considered concentrated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for relating the point to the body's weight.

rubric.why: This makes clear that the definition applies to the entire body.
rubric.description: States that the body's entire weight may be treated as acting at this single point.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the body's whole weight is represented at this point.

modelAnswer: The centre of gravity of a body is the point at which its whole weight is considered to act.

items.followUp: What is the moment of a force? Write its SI unit.

rubric.why: A couple consists of two forces that produce a turning effect.
rubric.description: Defines a couple as two equal, opposite, parallel forces acting at different points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the pair of forces and their arrangement.

rubric.why: A practical example demonstrates the action of a couple.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a couple.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as turning a steering wheel or a tap.

modelAnswer: A couple is a pair of equal and opposite parallel forces acting at different points, producing rotation.
Turning a steering wheel is an example of a couple.

items.followUp: Define kinetic energy and give its formula.

rubric.why: This is the definition of energy.
rubric.description: Defines energy as the capacity or ability to do work.

rubric.why: These are the two types of mechanical energy.
rubric.description: Names kinetic energy and potential energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both types.

modelAnswer: Energy is the capacity to do work.
The two types of mechanical energy are kinetic energy and potential energy.

items.followUp: Define pressure and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Stress is force per unit area, measured in pascals.
rubric.description: Defines stress and gives its SI unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for force per unit area and the unit pascal (Pa) or N/m².

rubric.why: Strain is a ratio of lengths, so it has no unit.
rubric.description: Defines strain as the ratio of change in dimension to original dimension and states that it has no unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition and its dimensionless nature.

modelAnswer: Stress is the force acting per unit area; its SI unit is the pascal (Pa), or N m⁻².
Strain is the ratio of the change in dimension to the original dimension; it has no unit.
